newsitem.title: USA: Texas separatists seize hostages, police close in.
newsitem.headline: Texas separatists seize hostages, police close in.

text.p: Armed separatists demanding independence for the state of Texas have seized two civilian hostages to press for the release of two jailed colleagues and FBI and police have moved in to surround their mountain compound.

Members of the self-designated Republic of Texas grabbed the hostages on Sunday in a nearby home after police arrested their chief of security, Bob Scheidt, on weapons possession charges when he left the compound in the Davis Mountains of southwest Texas.

Shots were fired and state officials said one hostage may have suffered a gunshot wound to the shoulder, although Republic members said he was only cut with flying glass and was not in serious condition.
FBI agents joined dozens of local and state police in surrounding the remote compound near the picturesque town of Fort Davis, about 80 miles (128 km) from the Mexican border.
By early evening, road blocks were set up and the group's telephone line had been disconnected to prevent its leaders from talking to the media or their outside supporters.
Republic of Texas leaders believe the state was annexed illegally in 1845 and claim it should be recognised as an independent nation with themselves as its leaders.
Richard McLaren, the group's leader and "ambassador," has been holed up in the remote compound since December, when an arrest warrant was issued against him on contempt of court charges.

Republic leaders began negotiations with police but said they would only hand over their hostages in exchange for the release of Scheidt and another Republic member who was recently arrested in Austin on contempt of court charges.
They are also demanding a state-wide referendum on whether Texas should declare itself an independent nation.

"We are not looking for anyone to die but if they have decided they want a war, they are going to get a war," said "White Eagle," the group's military liaison officer, in a telephone interview from inside the compound.
Scheidt was arrested early on Sunday when officers from the Jeff Davis County Sheriff's Department found two assault rifles in his van. He was in custody in a county jail late on Sunday.

White Eagle said the Republic had sealed its compound and ordered allied supporters to arrest and deport federal agents across Texas. "People are going to come out of the woodwork and take Texas back, they'll take the United States back too," he said.

McLaren says his group can call on thousands of supporters in any confrontation but police dispute those claims. It was not clear how many Republic members were holed up inside the modest compound, which was once a volunteer firehouse.

The group's hostages were Joe Rowe and his wife, M.A. Rowe, two neighbours at the centre of a bitter local property dispute with the Republic. An armed unit was keeping them hostage inside their own home, about 10 miles (16 km) away from McLaren's compound.
State government spokeswoman Lucila Torres said Joe Rowe had a broken arm and possibly a gunshot wound and was being treated inside the home by his wife, who is a paramedic.

Police set up road blocks to stop traffic in and out of the Fort Davis Resort subdivision where the compound and the Rowes' home are located. About 150 people are permanent residents of the subdivision but scores more have homes there.
White Eagle said the Rowes were prisoners of war and that their rights as defined under the Geneva Convention were being respected.

The Republic of Texas first emerged in 1995, demanding the resignation of Gov. George W. Bush and other state leaders as well as the removal of all federal agencies from Texas. It set up its own court system, which then issued a $93 trillion lien against the U.S. government, the United Nations and the Roman Catholic Church for allegedly plundering Texas' wealth.

State officials accuse the group of using millions of dollars of fraudulent cheques and filing thousands of bogus liens against government agencies and private property owners, tying up the courts with what state Attorney General Dan Morales has called "paper terrorism."
